🎙️ Ep. 61 of A guy with a scarf is out, with Julie Neenan Souza Souza, six years Global Head of Sports at Amazon Web Services (AWS) and now Executive in Residence at PwC.
Julie is someone I wanted on the show for a long time. While she carried the AWS badge it was never the right moment, and it got easier once she stepped away, which turned out to be the better version anyway, because the conversation went where it wanted to go, from a scrappy college sports startup to whether AI is making the next generation duller. We crossed paths at a lot of events over those years and I always admired the energy, and that on stage she brought her whole self, humour and opinions included, which is rare for someone carrying a badge that size.

Key points and quotes:
🪣 The three-bucket test for any technology project: the business problem, the solution deployed, and the outcome with a number on it. "If we can't explain it in three big buckets, then there's not a story there."
🕶️ The metaverse locker room a team asked AWS to build, and her first question: "Why do you want to do that?" She is seeing "we want an AI strategy" land in exactly the same shape now.
⏳ On measuring too early: "If you're looking for quick wins, you might have a few of those, but I don't think then you're using it to its full power either." The NFL kickoff rule was run through 10,000 simulated seasons before it changed.
🏈 "When I was at AWS, I wanted the big thorny problems."
🤝 On who should hold a multi-vendor solution together: "You want somebody you trust quarterbacking that." And on doing it all in-house: "If anybody's telling you they can do it all, that's probably not true."
🏁 On the argument that regulation means falling behind in the global race: "What are we racing toward? Like human extinction? Because I'm fine falling behind on that."
🧠 On AI and junior jobs: "How you know to make high judgment decisions is through experience." Stanford's August 2026 data has 22 to 25 year olds in AI-exposed jobs 19% behind their peers, with no gap for experienced workers.
🥱 On offloading your thinking to an agent: "I think you're going to be a more boring person."
🏟️ "I don't think live sports can be disintermediated."
And boy do I agree with that!!!

⚽ The season on YouTube so far: 106 days
Since 1 July the 101 club and league channels of Europe’s five big leagues have published 21,001 videos and collected 2.86 billion views. I took the YouTube Football Tracker’s season dashboards apart one chart at a time, for all five leagues together and for each league on its own, and published the six pages on my research hub.

📊 All five leagues
The Premier League has 1.1 billion views from 4,287 videos, La Liga 920 million from 6,626, so the league that publishes most earns second most, and an English upload is worth three and a half times an Italian one. Shorts carry every league, from 59% of views in England to 75% in France, and the shortest Shorts and the shortest long-form clips earn the most per video everywhere.
🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 The Premier League
The league channel sets the pace with Shorts that average close to a million views, Manchester City owns long-form at 745 thousand a video, and the five most consistent channels are the five biggest. A Brighton Short with 6.3 million views and 35 comments asks a question of its own.
🇪🇸 LALIGA
Barcelona and Real Madrid take 58% of the views, the league channel owns long-form, and Sevilla gets 96% of its views from Shorts. One Alavés Short is 79% of the club’s season, and Rayo Vallecano has published 22 videos in 106 days.
🇩🇪 Bundesliga
Bayern takes almost half of all Bundesliga views from fewer videos than the league channel, the clubs stream more than any other league and get the least for it, and the biggest video of the season is a referee’s microphone. The smaller clubs win on engagement, publish on the night and vanish for weeks at a time.
🇮🇹 Lega Serie A
Juventus sets the pace on Shorts, the league channel owns long-form, Inter publishes more than anyone and gets less per video, and Napoli goes silent for most of the season. One Como Short is the only one-hit wonder in the whole league.
🇫🇷 Ligue 1
PSG takes 70% of the views and the whole of the top eleven, with one eight-second Short at 44 million views, the league channel owns long-form, and nine clubs are silent on more than half the days of the season.

Netflix has bought the 2030 World Cup for Spain and Andorra, announced today with FIFA, and it will stream all 104 matches live, with one match per matchday free and a package with every Spain game, both semi-finals and the final going to a Spanish free-to-air channel that hasn’t been named yet.

I started in this business in 1987 and I have lost count of the times we said a streamer would never buy the biggest tournament in the world, in a country where football sits next to religion, and we said it with the same confidence we used for “nobody will watch a full match on a phone”. It happened anyway, the way most of those things happened, and it has a name, it’s called transformation.

Maybe Netflix is buying events and leaving league seasons to others, so the Serie A and Ligue 1 tenders he expects in the coming months probably won’t get a Netflix bid.
The free-to-air channel that gets the Spain package will be buying the national team from Netflix, and Netflix now decides what Spanish fans see for free during a home World Cup, which is a big shift for the Spanish TV market.

🛑 STOP Making This Mistake with Your API Strategy
I am sharing this because it truly resonates with my direct experience in streaming as a B2B vendor.

📺 Any streaming service that reaches some scale ends up living on a long list of devices, web, iOS, Android, Apple TV, Android TV, Fire TV, Roku, Samsung, LG, and the list grows with every distribution deal. Each of those apps is often built by a different team or partner, sometimes in a different language, and each one tends to carry its own copy of the rules the business runs on: who is entitled to what, which offer appears where, what happens when a subscription lapses, how a geo restriction applies to a given match. Those copies drift apart over time, so a fix lands on one platform weeks before it reaches another, and the product team spends a lot of its energy keeping ten apps in agreement with each other.

In the first clip from my conversation with Stephen Tallent, CEO of Mercury Intermedia, he goes straight at this:

 ⚙️ "So we feel it's pretty important to plan from the beginning to have all your platforms talking to the same APIs and provide as much of the business logic as possible there and really let the clients focus on the pixels. Let them focus on taking their time to make it look the way it needs to look, make it feel the way it needs to feel, making sure that user experience is great, and try to unify as much of the business logic as possible outside of the client, which saves time in some areas, takes a little longer in other areas. Again, if you plan for it, it can be done properly."

 📶 "Let the clients focus on the pixels" is the line I keep coming back to, because it gives the design and app teams back the work only they can do, how the thing feels on a 65-inch TV and on a phone on the bus, and it puts the rules that make money in one place where they get changed once. I also like that he names the cost, since some work gets slower and the payoff only comes if you decide it on day one, which is the exact decision most services skip when they are racing to get onto the next device.

 😎 Full disclosure, Mercury is a current client of A Guy With A Scarf.
The full episode is on the A Guy With A Scarf YouTube channel: https://lnkd.in/dqHguVBw
If your service runs on eight or more devices, where does your business logic live today, and how many copies of it are there?

▶️ A guy with a scarf NEW EPISODE
Could you run an in-house streaming platform without building every piece of it yourself, and swap an authentication, video or analytics vendor without touching a single client app?

🎙️ That is the question behind my conversation with Stephen Tallent, who founded Mercury Intermedia in 1996 and carries the CEO and CTO roles together. Mercury is a client of mine, so read this with that in mind, and I can vouch for what I saw on screen and what he said on the record.

1️⃣ Control of the endpoints your apps talk to. Stephen prefers the word control to ownership, and Quicksilver Stream keeps the business logic in one set of APIs so the apps can "focus on the pixels". His example is an authentication SDK dropped into every client app, which saves time on day one and lands the change in every app at once the day that vendor gets acquired.
2️⃣ No lock-in, including to Mercury. I challenged a vendor for saying it, and his answer was "if you provide a good product and you provide good service, they're gonna stay with you whether they have to or not". Customers keep their data, can swap any piece of the stack and can bring development in-house, which Stephen says a dozen customers have done with Mercury. He also named the tension himself: the customer needs control and the vendor needs to make money.
3️⃣ A producer builds a page by asking for it, no box-ticking and menu-scrolling. In the demo I described a feature I wanted, a producer testing a new page layout in plain language, and the team did it in front of me on the working platform. I had thought my idea was clever and it already existed, so I felt a mix of embarrassment and surprise.
One of the most clever use of AI I have seen in a B2B product so far. Great news for streaming platform producer teams.

What intrigued me about Quicksilver Stream is that it is not yet-another-streaming-platform. It sits between the client apps and the vendors a customer chooses, so video platform, or an authentication provider can change underneath it.

10 Things To Consider about the second Genius Sports CEO letter 📝
In March I wrote about Mark Locke's first letter, the one defending the $1.2 billion Legend deal. Seven months later there is a second one, "Americans are Going to Keep Wagering", and this time the subject is prediction markets. Same format, same footnotes, same forward-looking statements notice at the bottom, and the same audience: investors asking what happens to Genius if the courts or Congress take sports contracts away from Kalshi and Polymarket.

His point in one sentence 🎯 Americans will keep wagering on sport whatever the courts decide, and Genius gets paid however that wagering is routed, because it supplies the exchanges, the market makers behind them and the sportsbooks competing with them for the same customer. The rules decide who pays Genius; the demand, in his telling, guarantees that someone does.

The 🔟 things to consider:
1️⃣ It is an investor document that happens to be on LinkedIn, written while the Kalshi cases and the Supreme Court petition are still open.
2️⃣ The thesis separates the demand for wagering from the structure that carries it, and never describes a scenario in which Genius loses.
3️⃣ Settlement is where he is strongest: the Western Michigan at Michigan market on 5 September, $18.6 million paid out on a broadcast clock that had one second put back.
4️⃣ The economics claim, that an exchange dollar pays Genius as well as a sportsbook dollar, "match or exceed" in his words, has no public number under it.
5️⃣ Two Eilers & Krejcik percentages, 69 per cent and 2 per cent, carry the whole "net benefit" argument, and DraftKings and FanDuel read the same monitor.
6️⃣ The politics paragraph names Donald Trump Jr. and Stephanie Cutter in the same breath as a bipartisan bill to ban the contracts, which is more candid than the format usually allows.
7️⃣ Connecticut's subpoenas have two Genius entities on the list, and the letter gets past that in two sentences.
8️⃣ The February letter and this one are one argument in two parts, and Prediction.com launched two days later to prove it.
9️⃣ The timing tells you what the letter is for: after Q2, after the exchange deals, in the first NFL season with real exchange volume, built to be quoted back in a year.
🔟 What is missing: Sportradar, the leagues, the taxes already in force in Illinois and coming in North Carolina, and anywhere outside the US.

For paid members there is an appendix 📎 with the company timeline from Betgenius in 2001 to Prediction.com, four years of financials with the three 2026 guidance revisions side by side, the Legend deal terms, and a short Mark Locke bio built only on what I could source.

Do you buy the settlement argument, and would you believe "match or exceed" before seeing a number? Share what you think 👇

⚽ 🤖 FIFA wants fan journey tech for the Women’s World Cup 2027, next-generation wearables and connected substitution boards.

Earlier this year, at the Bundesliga SportsInnovation event in Düsseldorf, I shared a stage with Nicolas Evans from FIFA, talking 3D data, officiating and the Football Technology Centre, and what stayed with me was how much of FIFA's innovation work now runs through structured channels rather than conversations in a hospitality box.

This week those channels opened three new doors. The FIFA Innovation Programme has published three challenges:
⚽ Fan journey technology for the FIFA Women's World Cup 2027 in Brazil, which FIFA says is its first innovation challenge tied to a specific competition. Applications close on 1 November 2026, and the criteria ask for a fully operational solution already delivered across multiple projects, commercial partner integration and measurable ROI. Four weeks is short, but count backwards from kick-off on 24 June 2027 through FIFA's five-step process and there is little other room to deploy anything.
⚽ Next-generation sports wearables, measuring hydration, load, recovery and stress in real time. Working prototype minimum, no deadline, with validation through FIFA's research partners and academic institutions on offer.
⚽ Connected substitution boards, hardware that links to the substitution software FIFA already runs and shows player numbers to the stadium. Lightweight, durable, three hours of battery, manual fallback, working prototype minimum, no deadline.

All three go through the same portal, which runs on a video pitch platform, so expect to pitch on camera.

If you run fan journey, ticketing, accessibility or in-stadium technology that is already live with reputable clients, the Women's World Cup brief is written for you and the clock is running, so apply. If you build wearables or match operations hardware, the other two are open with no deadline, so get your prototype evidence in order and go. Know a company that fits one of the three? Fanatics Betting & Gaming's CTO on Building a Sportsbook With AI
Ian Botts in conversation with Nick Meacham (SportsPro CEO) at SportsPro AI and Tech 2026

Ian Botts runs technology for Fanatics Betting & Gaming, about 920 engineers by his count, gave the funniest, which at an AI conference at 9:30 is a public service.

My take: he did the rollout in the right order, and almost nobody does. AI went inside the tools people already used, then a platform made the model a swappable part, and only after that did agents go in front of customers. The usual conference version starts with the customer-facing demo and ends with a slide.

A few lines worth keeping:
"What problem am I trying to solve?" His answer when the industry told everyone to adopt AI.
"I'm nothing but Claude from here to eternity," followed a breath later by "who knows what's going to happen tomorrow." Which is why he built the platform model-agnostic.
"Engineers are problem solvers. Writing code is a very small part of building software that is either at scale, works correctly, or God forbid, is actually secure."
And on his own coding: he has not shipped production code in a decade, and was asked to stop when it got bad.

The full piece on A guy with a scarf covers:
🤖 The sportsbook as a spreadsheet, and why Fanatics bets on FanCash instead of bonuses
🤖 The adoption numbers (4.7 days a week for engineers) and what they do and do not tell you
🤖 Meemaw and Daisy, the two agents in production, one beside support staff and one building bet slips in chat
🤖 Fuel, the reuse library behind a prediction market built in 100 days
🤖 My reservation about measuring habit instead of outcomes

Paid subscribers also get the appendices: Fanatics' three businesses with 2024 revenue by segment, the financials I could source and the ones I could not, a timeline from GSI Commerce to Ontario, and Ian's bio. Those took longer to check than the article took to write.

🤖 What a Broadcaster, a Content Platform and a Video Infrastructure Vendor Say About Building a Sports Media Stack for AI

Sean Hunter of Fox, Daniel Kirschner of Greenfly and Chris Wilson of MediaKind on the panel I moderated at SportsPro AI and Tech 2026.

Yesterday I noticed a lot of sports people explaining AI and a lot of AI people explaining sports, so I picked a broadcaster, a content operations platform and a video infrastructure vendor and asked each to stay in their own field.
Sean said the data team at Fox now works directly with journalists and commentators, and data scientists "exist in greater numbers even than before." Fox shipped an ElevenLabs feature for the World Cup where fans put questions to Colin Cowherd, a "catch me up with the highlights" video pipeline, and announced agentic ad buying at Cannes Lions. His warning on AI features: "if you just sort of stick a chat box onto an existing product, no one knows what that's for."
Daniel, on the idea that AI makes building easier: "you can build a lot more and a lot more complex things and a lot more effective things." He compared it to spreadsheets, which people expected to end accountants. Greenfly says 25,000 athletes use its app. His view of Europe against the US: Europe asks where to store content, and the US asks how to make money on it.
Chris described how MediaKind, now combined with Harmonic, exposes its platform through MCP so that "Greenfly can plug in their agent and drive our video pipe," and Fox can do the same. On the pace of change: "Some of those models will not be here in three months," so the value is in being able to swap them and fail fast.
I closed on a sour note, since nobody has cracked fan engagement yet. Daniel's reply: "I don't think it's a solvable problem." Sean agreed. And everyone means something different when they say fan engagement.

quoted_post.author: Carlo De Marchis
quoted_post.text:
I spent day one of SportsPro AI + Tech at London Stadium and posted notes from the floor all day.
A question I asked myself on the way out: have I learned something new?
Meh, not really. But do I have a better understanding of what our ecosystem is doing in AI and tech, what people are thinking, trying, doing, succeeding at and failing at? Definitely yes.
So, a good day for me.

The sessions worth remembering were the ones where somebody said what didn’t work, why they stopped, or how long it took before anything paid off.
I appreciate those who put the people involved at the centre of any solution, not in a romantic way, but because, as with every process, if people are not properly on board, the results are rarely positive.
I say this with humility and respect (as someone who wanders around town with the laptop open in his hands, because there is always a Claude Code session running): sometimes it felt like people from Sports were “lecturing” us about AI, and people from the AI world were explaining sport to us. I guess it’s a very human (not artificial) way of reassuring the audience that they get it, when in reality they are just starting a journey. No need for that. Let’s all do something more useful: let’s double down on what we are experts in (if anything, in my case) and share what we have learned, including what failed, and the half-formed ideas we would bet on, so that somebody in the room holding the other half can pick them up.

One thing I observed is that we went from AI as magic, “look what I did with it”, to the “AI needs to serve a business objective” mantra, or mood.
Good. But...
The same question kept coming back on stage all day: should you start with the technology or with a business problem? I couldn’t take a position, because I think the question is wrong, or at least neither answer solves it. If I start from a business problem without knowing what the technology can now do differently, I won’t see the problem at all, since my very human brain doesn’t register something as a problem until it has a hint that it can be solved at all, and starting from the technology gives you demos and pilots that die quietly. Tech and business have to be a conversation, and I’ve lived that for most of my career: technical people need to understand the business at least well enough to know which problems are worth their time, business people need to understand the technology at least well enough to imagine what has become possible, and the two sides progress and innovate together.
😎 That is my take.

posts.text: 10 Things To Consider after Cloudflare turned 16 and the CEO's letter

quoted_post.author: Carlo De Marchis
quoted_post.text:
10 Things To Consider after Cloudflare turned 16 and the CEO's letter

💌 Cloudflare's 2026 founders' letter, signed by CEO Matthew Prince and co-founder Michelle Zatlyn, says machines now make more requests on the web than people do, and projects 1,000 times more within five years. Here is what that means for sports media, rights holders and the vendors who sell to them.

I saw Dan Rayburn's post about the letter on Saturday night and got hooked. Some of this is technical, and I wrote it so anyone in the industry can follow.

1️⃣ The bot crossover arrived eighteen months early, and the company with the widest view of web traffic missed its own forecast by more than a year
2️⃣ Agent traffic shows up on the hosting bill first: a fan asks one question, a dozen sports sites pay to answer it, one gets the click
3️⃣ Page views were already a weak currency for sponsor reports and agents make them weaker, in both directions
4️⃣ Since 15 September, new sites with ads block AI agents by default, with separate switches for search, AI training and AI agents
5️⃣ Sports already has a pricing model for machines, in official data feeds sold to bookmakers, which most publishers are only starting to build
6️⃣ Italy and Spain made Cloudflare the villain of the piracy fight, with a €14.2 million AGCOM fine, LaLiga blocking 3,000 IPs a weekend and collateral damage on both sides
7️⃣ Agents tend to recommend whoever is already known, which is bad news for every young sports-tech vendor with a better product and a thinner footprint
8️⃣ The CEO thinks credibility will beat popularity, and the formats an agent has to cite by name are the ones that keep their value
9️⃣ A fifth of the web sits behind one company, which is convenient until it writes your crawler policy or goes down on a matchday
🔟 Cloudflare cut its "measurers" and kept building, and sports organisations are heavy on measurers

🤖 My position: treat agent access as a rights product, priced and licensed with the same seriousness as a betting feed, and tell sponsors plainly which part of the audience is people, which part is machines and which part never visited because an agent answered for them. If you are working on either of those problems, get in touch. I want to compare notes.

quoted_post.author: Ben Swanton
quoted_post.text:
A few people picked up on the last point in my IBC post, that almost everyone is hiring to an ownership clock. Carlo De Marchis asked me to go deeper, so here it is.

I wrote recently that candidates should diligence the cap table before they sign. This is the other side of that.

Most hiring briefs describe a job. Very few describe the clock it is being hired into, and the clock usually decides whether the hire works.

Year two of a hold period and year four are different jobs with the same title. In year two you are hiring someone to build: new markets, new segments, a team that will take three years to mature. In year four you are hiring someone who can produce a clean, defensible growth story on a timeline that is already set, in a business where half the leadership team is watching for the exit. Both are legitimate. They are not the same person, and a good year-two hire can fail badly in year four.

A founder-owned business with no exit pressure can hire for a decade. A business with a strategic minority holder whose intentions are unresolved often cannot hire at all, because nobody wants to commit budget before the ownership question settles. That hesitation is itself a decision, and it usually costs more than the hire would have.

Here is what I see that most people outside the process do not. The brief a company starts with is frequently not the brief the person is eventually hired against.

That is rarely indecision. It is the clock moving. A board conversation happens, an approach arrives, a plan gets pulled forward or pushed back, and the profile shifts underneath the search. A build mandate quietly becomes a scale mandate. A regional role becomes a global one. The title stays the same and everyone carries on as though nothing changed.

Handled well, that is a good thing. A search that runs over weeks forces conversations a single planning meeting never gets to, and companies often end up hiring something better than they first described. Handled badly, the candidate is the last to know and starts the job working to a brief that expired before they signed.

The practical version: before you open a senior search, answer two questions honestly between you and your board. What has to be true about this business in 24 months, and who needs to be convinced of it. Then revisit both as the process runs, and tell the shortlist when the answers change.

If you are hiring senior commercial leadership at the moment, whose clock are you really working to?

🔟❓Attempts to answer those 10 questions I had for IBC 2026 ⁉️
Two weeks ago I published the ten questions I was taking to IBC 2026.
I promised myself I would come back and answer every one of them, including the ones where the answer is that I still do not know.
My take on the show first: 🟩 quality over quantity, 🟩 less posturing, 🟨 fat portfolio syndrome (everybody now offers everything), and 🟨 a tough market for everyone where sport moved even further centre stage.

My 10 almost answers:
1️⃣ Market or calendar? Answered. The exceptional year raised the bar, and sport is now the workload everybody designs against.
2️⃣ DAZN eating the world? Answered, with a twist. Yes, and the DTC apps left standing are run by people who did the homework. Only the brave are left.
3️⃣ Fixing what fans complain about? Partly. Ads are moving, discovery is stuck, price is sliding, and buffering is the one I am losing hope on.
4️⃣ Fan insight reaching production? Partly, and the one I am most encouraged by. The OBS drones at Milano Cortina were built because fans asked to feel closer. That is the second case after vertical video.
5️⃣ Demo to deployment? Answered, and the answer is a new problem. AI coding shortened both paths and gave us a confused market where nobody knows which of a vendor's twelve modules is the good one.
6️⃣ AI as cover or as the job? Halfway. AI slop went front page this summer, so posturing gets spotted by everyone now, and vendors adjusted.
7️⃣ Who runs the tools? Open. Everybody says human in the loop, and the phrase covers two very different states: deliberate control, or a tool that is not ready.
8️⃣ Nobody publishes the numbers? Open, no progress. The only public metric this industry has is what survives, with a two-year lag.
9️⃣ Bottom line or top line? 75/25 by my own reading, and the 25 now comes with a serious attempt to show where the revenue comes from. Overdue.
🔟 What is the buy side buying? Open, and I will not pretend otherwise. One observation from my corner: clients came looking for innovation that makes a measurable difference, and they came prepared to evaluate it.

Four answered, three partly, three open, and the open ones are all about evidence and accountability. The tools got better, the marketing got more truthful, the buyers got more serious, and the industry still cannot show its own numbers.
If you read any of these ten differently, tell me. If you are on the buy side and can correct question 10, tell me twice.
I was there for Dolby OptiView and also represented Mercury Intermedia.

🏃‍♀️‍➡️ The World Record Film turns the whole history of athletics records into cards you flip through — one film for the men, one for the women, 33 cards each.

🏃‍♂️‍➡️ My love for athletics started when i was a kid, Pietro Mennea, Dwight Stones, etc… then professionally in 1991 when I worked more than one year for the Tokyo World Championships and saw the magic of Carl Lewis and Mike Powell world record.

🏃 Two films — men and women, 33 cards each, in World Athletics' own event order.
📈 The staircase — every mark that ever held the record; the width of each step is how long it survived.
👻 The ghost race — press play and every era runs at once. Bolt crosses the line 9.6 m ahead of 1912.
🕳️ The pit — jumps and throws laid out at the distance they actually went, oldest at the back.
❓ Cards that explain themselves — why a ratified record sometimes goes backwards: hand timing, rule changes, a redesigned javelin.
📊 Stats for one event — nations, athletes, age and reign length, narrowed to the card you're on.
🌍 Nations — who owned each record, year by year. The USA held the 100 m for 77 of its 114 years.
🏅 Where records fall — every record as a dot, gold for the Olympics, cyan for the Worlds, grey for everywhere else. Grey wins.
📅 Records per day — all 1,382 marks on a 366-day calendar. 84.5% fall between May and September; 106 days have never produced one.
🎂 Age — how old they were, with a decade slider to watch it move.
⏳ How long records last — the longest reigns ever, each drawn from the day it was set to the day it fell.
⚖️ One ranking, men and women — every standing record in a single list. The oldest is 43 years old.
🔗 Every card has its own link — and it reloads exactly where you left off.

❓ What if there is another way to buy a streaming tech stack?
Own the platform, rent the expertise, keep the right to change your mind on every supplier.

🤖 I spent most of my career on the vendor side of streaming. At every renewal the same clients asked the same two questions. Can we own more of this? Can we depend on you less? I answered with contract clauses. Exit terms, data export, an escrow nobody opened. They rented, we held the keys.

📰 A few months ago I wrote about consolidation narrowing choice and ownership coming back as a buying criterion. A team in Nashville/NYC called me, read a few of my sentences back to me and said this is what we are building. That team is Mercury Intermedia. They announced Quicksilver Stream this week. I advise them, paid, so read me as interested.
What those clients were asking for, and what an in-house streaming platform gives them:

🎛️ Control. The decisions about the platform sit on the client's side of the table.💰 Investment. Fees accumulate into an asset instead of expiring with each contract.
🔌 Pluggable vendors. DRM, payments, data, ads swapped at the server side, apps untouched.
🛡️ Security. A platform that survives whatever happens to the company that built it.
📈 A long horizon. A stack that grows with the business instead of forcing a rebuild every four or five years.

The counter-arguments are real and they are in the article. Ownership without operational excellence is a marketing word. A license plus support looks like SaaS, until the vendor gets bought and only one of you keeps a platform. Control has a running cost. The price is capital, and the same buyers sign three-year SaaS deals worth more.

I understand this model may not be for everybody. It makes a lot of sense for rights holders and media brands that expect to be running their own audience relationship in ten years and want agency over the thing that runs it.

A guy with a scarf asks a question to...
Untangling MoQ with Jan Ozer

Latency is the debate that comes back every trade show and rarely gets interesting. While putting together my 10 questions for IBC 2026 I kept running into three letters, MoQ, so I asked the person I trust most on codecs and delivery, Jan Ozer, to explain what it is and why anyone in sports should care.

What Jan told me, in his words:
1️⃣ "MoQ stands for Media over QUIC. It's a new way to deliver live video over the internet with less than a second of delay, even when the audience is very large."
2️⃣ "Today, to achieve low latency in a broadcast setting, streaming platforms generally choose between two imperfect options."
3️⃣ "WebRTC provides extremely low latency and works well for interactive applications like video calls, telehealth and remote control. But WebRTC is designed primarily for two-way communication. Distributing a WebRTC stream to millions of viewers requires specialized servers and substantial infrastructure. It's too expensive for general broadcasts like the Super Bowl or the World Cup."
4️⃣ "HLS and DASH handle one-to-many broadcasting very efficiently and work well with existing content delivery networks. But even their low latency versions typically remain several seconds behind the action."
5️⃣ "MoQ is designed to fill the gap between them. It's primarily for one-to-many broadcasting, not two-way interaction."
6️⃣ "A broadcaster publishes a stream. Viewers subscribe to the stream. And relay servers distribute copies from locations close to the viewers. A relay can receive one copy of the stream and pass it to many viewers, much like a conventional content delivery network."
7️⃣ "That gives MoQ the real-time performance associated with WebRTC and the massive scale associated with HLS and DASH."
8️⃣ "The most obvious markets are live sports betting, auctions, gaming and other large events where even a few seconds of delay can spoil the experience. If your neighbor cheers before you see the goal, or the betting market changes before your video catches up, latency matters."
9️⃣ "MoQ is still an emerging standard. Products and early deployments exist, but the specification and supporting ecosystem are not yet finished."
🔟 "MoQ is not replacing WebRTC, HLS or DASH tomorrow. But it may eventually provide something the industry has always wanted: real-time one-to-many broadcasting at internet scale and affordable costs."
